Note: Complete Technical Details can be found in the IRF540N datasheet given at the end of this page.

The IRF540N is an N-Channel Mosfet. This mosfet can drive loads upto 23A and can support peak current upto 110A. It also has a threshold voltage of 4V, which means it can easily driven by low voltages like 5V. Hence it is mostly used with Arduino and other microcontrollers for logic switching. Speed control of motors and Light dimmers are also possible with this Mosfet since it has good switching characteristics.
So if you are looking for a Mosfet to switch applications that consume high current with some logic level devices, then this Mosfet will be a perfect choice for you.

Unlike transistors, MOSFETs are voltage controlled devices. Meaning, they can be turned on or turned off by supplying the required Gate threshold voltage (VGS). IRF540N is an N-channel MOSFET, so the Drain and Source pins will be left open when there is no voltage applied to the gate pin. When a gate voltage is applied these pins gets closed.

The below circuit shows how this mosfet behaves when the Gate voltage is applied (5V) and not applied (0V). Since this an N-Channel mosfet the load that has to be switched (in this case a motor) should always be connected above the drain pin.

When you turn on a Mosfet by supplying the required voltage to the gate pin, it will remain on unless you supply 0V to the gate. To avoid this problem, we should always use a pull-down resistor (R1), here I have used a value of 10k. In applications like controlling the speed of motor or dimming a light we would use a PWM signal for fast switching, during this scenario, the MOSFET’s gate capacitance will create a reverse current due to parasitic effect. To tackle this we should use a current limiting capacitor, I have used a value of 470 here.

This I2C 1602 LCD display shows 2 lines of 16 characters on a blue backlight, using an HD44780-compatible controller with a soldered I2C interface. Instead of wiring 6 or more data pins directly to a microcontroller, this module connects with just two wires (SDA and SCL) — freeing up I/O pins for sensors, buttons, or other modules on the same Arduino, ESP32, or Raspberry Pi project.
How the I2C Interface Simplifies Wiring

A standard HD44780 character LCD normally needs 6 to 11 digital pins to drive it directly, which is often more than a small board like an Arduino UNO can spare alongside other components. The I2C backpack soldered onto this IIC LCD 2x16 module (built around a PCF8574-type chip) reduces that down to just two lines — SDA and SCL — plus power and ground. That leaves far more pins free for sensors, motors, or other displays on the same project.
Default I2C address: typically 0x27 (or 0x3F on some batches) — the same address range used across most PCF8574-based 1602/2004 LCD backpacks.
Changeable address: solder pads (commonly labeled A0/A1/A2) allow the address to be changed, so more than one I2C device can share the same two-wire bus without conflicting.
Onboard contrast control: a small potentiometer on the backpack adjusts character visibility — if the screen looks blank, this is usually the first thing to check.
Backlight control: a jumper on the backpack switches the backlight on or off; removing it lets the backlight be powered or controlled separately.
What Can You Display on a 2x16 Character LCD?

With 2 rows of 16 characters, this I2C LCD for Arduino projects and similar boards is enough to show short status messages, sensor readings, or menu prompts — not graphics, but plenty for most hobby and educational projects:
Sensor readings (temperature, humidity, distance) updated in real time.
Simple menus or status messages for a project with buttons or a rotary encoder.
Clock/date displays when paired with an RTC module.
Debug output during development, without needing the Serial Monitor connected.
Need a small graphical display instead of character-only text? RAM's 0.96" OLED I2C Display Module uses the same two-wire I2C interface but can show simple graphics and icons, not just characters.
What does "I2C" mean on this LCD?

I2C (also written IIC) is a two-wire communication protocol. Instead of wiring many separate data pins to the display, the microcontroller talks to it over just two lines — SDA (data) and SCL (clock) — which this module's soldered-on backpack handles.
What is the default I2C address of this display?
Most PCF8574-based 1602 I2C backpacks default to address 0x27 (some ship as 0x3F). If unsure, a simple I2C scanner sketch (widely available for Arduino) will report the exact address.
How many pins does it need to connect to a microcontroller?
Just four: VCC, GND, SDA, and SCL — compared to 6 or more pins for a standard parallel HD44780 LCD.
Is it compatible with Arduino, ESP32, and Raspberry Pi?
Yes — any board with an I2C-capable interface (SDA/SCL pins) can drive it, including Arduino UNO/Nano/Mega, ESP32/ESP8266 boards, and Raspberry Pi.
Can I change the I2C address if I need to connect more than one device?
Yes — solder pads on the backpack (usually labeled A0/A1/A2) let you change the address so multiple I2C devices, including more than one LCD, can share the same two-wire bus.
Does it need a special library to work?
Yes — libraries such as LiquidCrystal_I2C (Arduino) handle the I2C communication and character display, and are widely available and well documented for this exact type of module.

Its slim, handheld shape gives it the feel of a test probe; you press it against the curved side of a gas cylinder, and it communicates its reading via LED lights. Its build is designed for quick checks, not precision measurement, but for everyday use it bridges convenience and function.

When in use, you position the probe perpendicularly against different heights on the gas bottle. The unit emits ultrasonic pulses inward, detects reflections, and determines whether liquid is present at that level. Then the LED indicator lights green if liquid is present, red if not, or flashes during measurement. There’s a built-in flashlight to assist when ambient light is low, such as in darker kitchens, storage rooms, or outdoor BBQ settings. The measurement feedback is immediate, giving the user a quick sense of where the fill level lies.

In practice, the UT345C becomes a useful tool for households, gas retailers, restaurants, or campsites that rely on LPG tanks. Rather than guessing or tipping tanks, you can quickly scan levels at multiple points. Its simplicity no need for calibration, no complicated readouts makes it effective for nontechnical users. Over time, it reduces waste, ensures timely refills, and helps avoid situations where a tank runs dry unexpectedly.

Playback channels include a built-in equalizer switch to select between normal and metal tape types, while recording channels feature an automatic level control (ALC) detector to maintain consistent output levels despite varying input amplitudes.

The Heat Bed High Power MOSFET Module 25A is designed to safely control high-current heated beds in 3D printers. Instead of passing the full heated-bed current through the printer motherboard, the module draws power directly from the external power supply.

The printer control board only sends the switching signal. Therefore, the heavy electrical load passes through the external MOSFET module. This arrangement helps reduce stress on motherboard terminals, connectors, and onboard MOSFET components.

The module supports common 12V and 24V 3D-printer systems. In addition, its large aluminum heatsink improves heat dissipation during operation. It is especially useful when installing a larger heated bed or replacing a standard bed with a higher-power model.

Connect the external power supply to the module’s power-input terminals. Next, connect the heated bed to the output terminals. Finally, connect the supplied control cable between the MOSFET signal input and the heated-bed output on the printer motherboard.
The positive and negative polarity markings must be followed carefully. Furthermore, the power supply voltage must match the rated voltage of the heated bed.

The 25A value is the module’s maximum rating and should not be treated as a guaranteed continuous current under every installation condition. Continuous high-current operation may require additional airflow or a 30mm cooling fan.

blocks.text: The Arduino Uno R3 is a open source microcontroller board based on the ATmega328 chip. This Board has 14 digital input/output pins, 6 analog input pins, Onboard 16 MHz ceramic resonator, Port for USB connection, Onboard DC power jack, An ICSP header and a microcontroller reset button. It contains everything needed to support the microcontroller. Using the board is also very easy, simply connect it to a computer with a USB cable or power it with DC adapter or battery to get started.

The Uno differs from all preceding boards in that it does not use the FTDI USB-to-serial driver chip. Instead, it features the Atmega16U2Atmega8U2 up to version R2) programmed as a USB-to-serial converter. While the Arduino UNO can be powered via the USB connection or with an external power supply, the power source is selected automatically.

External (non-USB) power can come either from an AC-to-DC adapter (wall-wart) or battery. The adapter can be connected by plugging a 2.1mm center-positive plug into the board’s power jack. Also leads from a battery can be inserted in the Gnd and Vin pin headers of the Power connector. The board can operate on an external supply of 6 to 20 volts. If supplied with less than 7V, however, the 5V pin may supply less than five volts and the board may be unstable. If using more than 12V, the voltage regulator may overheat and damage the board. The recommended range is 5v to 12v for Arduino Uno.

blocks.text: The LM35 module is a precision temperature sensor that outputs an analog voltage directly proportional to the Celsius temperature scale. The module typically includes the LM35 IC alongside supporting passive components, offering a simple interface for temperature measurement.

Operating with a voltage range of 4-20V DC, the sensor draws a low quiescent current of less than 60µA, ensuring minimal power consumption. Its output voltage changes by 10mV per degree Celsius, enabling direct reading without complex mathematical conversions. The sensor’s linear scale and predictable response make it suitable for a wide range of thermal monitoring applications where accuracy and stability are prioritized over absolute precision.
